title: Habakkuk 2:6–20
context: The LORD’s answer continues with a taunt song that the oppressed nations take up against the plunderer (2:6). Five woes follow: against extortion and plunder (2:6–8), against evil gain that seeks a nest on high (2:9–11), against a city built with blood (2:12–14), against making a neighbor drunk to shame him (2:15–17), and against idols that cannot speak (2:18–19). Each woe turns the oppressor’s deeds back on him, measure for measure. In the middle stands a promise: “the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the LORD’s glory, as the waters cover the sea” (2:14). Isaiah 11:9 uses very similar language in its own setting, and the two are named here without being merged. The images of drunkenness and exposure in 2:15–16 picture the humiliation of conquered nations, and these notes treat them soberly. The chapter closes with the LORD in his holy temple and all the earth silent before him (2:20). Babylon is most likely in view throughout, though the woes are phrased so that they apply to any power that behaves this way. Shared ground: both traditions read the woes as God’s just verdict on violence, greed, and idolatry, and both see the LORD’s glory, not empire, as the destiny of the earth.

verses.text: Won’t all these take up a parable against him, and a taunting proverb against him, and say, ‘Woe to him who increases that which is not his, and who enriches himself by extortion! How long?’
verses.arminianNotes: “Won’t all these take up a parable against him?” The nations Babylon oppressed now taunt it. Arminian readers see justice reversing roles: the plunderer “who increases that which is not his” becomes the object of mockery, and the cry “How long?” echoes the prophet’s own.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s justice voiced through the victims, so that the woes are not mere revenge but the LORD’s verdict on extortion. Shared ground: both traditions read the five woes as a taunt song announcing the downfall of the oppressor, and both hear “How long?” as linking the nations’ cry with Habakkuk’s in 1:2.

verses.text: Won’t your debtors rise up suddenly, and wake up those who make you tremble, and you will be their victim?
verses.arminianNotes: “Won’t your debtors rise up suddenly?” Arminian readers see the consequences of exploitation coming back on the exploiter: those he oppressed become the means of his downfall, a fitting outcome of cruelty freely chosen.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the sudden reversal as God’s providential justice, which makes the oppressor “their victim” at the time he appoints. Shared ground: both traditions read the “debtors” as those whom Babylon plundered or held in its grip, and both see the reversal as just recompense rather than mere change of fortune.

verses.text: Because you have plundered many nations, all the remnant of the peoples will plunder you because of men’s blood, and for the violence done to the land, to the city and to all who dwell in it.
verses.arminianNotes: “Because you have plundered many nations, all the remnant of the peoples will plunder you.” Arminian readers stress the measure-for-measure principle: what the plunderer did will be done to him, “because of men’s blood” and the violence done to land and city.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see retributive justice built into God’s moral order, applied to empires as surely as to individuals. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as poetic justice, note that it repeats the language of violence from 1:2–3 and 1:9, and see God as the one who ensures that oppression is repaid in kind.

verses.text: Woe to him who gets an evil gain for his house, that he may set his nest on high, that he may be delivered from the hand of evil!
verses.arminianNotes: “Woe to him who gets an evil gain for his house, that he may set his nest on high.” Arminian readers see the futility of seeking security through unjust gain: the plunderer tries to place himself beyond “the hand of evil,” yet his gains invite ruin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the nest on high as pride seeking self-made safety, the opposite of the righteous who live by faith in 2:4. Shared ground: both traditions read the second woe as condemning the pursuit of security through exploitation, and both note the irony that the high nest offers no true protection from the judgment of God.

verses.text: You have devised shame to your house by cutting off many peoples, and have sinned against your soul.
verses.arminianNotes: “You have devised shame to your house by cutting off many peoples, and have sinned against your soul.” Arminian readers see self-destruction in the choice: the plan meant to build up his house brings shame on it and harms his own life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that sin against others is also sin against oneself, and that the shame of the house is God’s verdict on its violence. Shared ground: both traditions read “sinned against your soul” as meaning that the oppressor forfeits his own life and well-being, and both see the scheme as self-defeating from the start.

verses.text: For the stone will cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the woodwork will answer it.
verses.arminianNotes: “For the stone will cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the woodwork will answer it.” Arminian readers hear the materials of the house built by injustice bearing witness against its owner, so that nothing done in secret stays hidden.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image as God’s insistence that hidden injustice will be exposed, since even stone and timber give testimony. Shared ground: both traditions read the personification as poetry of accusation, and some readers compare Jesus’ words about stones crying out in Luke 19:40, a connection named without merging the two settings.

verses.text: Woe to him who builds a town with blood, and establishes a city by iniquity!
verses.arminianNotes: “Woe to him who builds a town with blood, and establishes a city by iniquity!” Arminian readers see the third woe condemning civic and imperial projects founded on violence, and stress that the builders bear responsibility for the cost in lives.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the city built by iniquity as a picture of every human kingdom raised against God, destined to fall before his reign. Shared ground: both traditions read the woe as condemning bloodshed and oppression in empire building, and both see the verse as preparing for the contrast with the LORD’s glory in verse 14.

verses.text: Behold, isn’t it from the LORD of Armies that the peoples labor for the fire, and the nations weary themselves for vanity?
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, isn’t it from the LORD of Armies that the peoples labor for the fire?” Arminian readers see God’s judgment making unjust labor futile: what is built by oppression is destined for fire, and nations “weary themselves for vanity.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that the futility is “from the LORD of Armies”: he determines that projects raised against his justice come to nothing. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as declaring the emptiness of empire built on blood, compare similar language in Jeremiah 51:58, and see the LORD as sovereign over the outcome of human labor.

verses.text: For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the LORD’s glory, as the waters cover the sea.
verses.arminianNotes: “For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the LORD’s glory, as the waters cover the sea.” Arminian readers hear a universal hope: in contrast to cities built with blood, God’s purpose is a world filled with the knowledge of his glory, open to all nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the certainty of God’s purpose: the glory of the LORD, not Babylon’s, will fill the earth as surely as the waters cover the sea. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the hope at the center of the woes, and both note that Isaiah 11:9 uses very similar language in a different setting, a parallel named without merging the two.

verses.text: “Woe to him who gives his neighbor drink, pouring your inflaming wine until they are drunk, so that you may gaze at their naked bodies!
verses.arminianNotes: “Woe to him who gives his neighbor drink.” The fourth woe uses the image of making another drunk in order to shame them. Arminian readers see the deliberate degradation of others, probably a picture of how Babylon humiliated subject nations, and they treat the image soberly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image as exposing the cruelty of power that delights in another’s disgrace, and read it chiefly as a figure for imperial humiliation. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly, see the drinking and exposure as an image of nations stripped and shamed, and acknowledge that it may also reflect real abuses without dwelling on them.

verses.text: You are filled with shame, and not glory. You will also drink and be exposed! The cup of the LORD’s right hand will come around to you, and disgrace will cover your glory.
verses.arminianNotes: “You are filled with shame, and not glory.” The one who shamed others will be shamed. Arminian readers see “The cup of the LORD’s right hand will come around to you” as fitting judgment: what the oppressor forced on others returns to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the cup as a familiar prophetic image of God’s wrath (compare Jeremiah 25:15), now passed to Babylon by the LORD’s own right hand. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as measure-for-measure judgment, see the cup as God’s just response to cruelty, and note the contrast between shame here and the glory of verse 14.

verses.text: For the violence done to Lebanon will overwhelm you, and the destruction of the animals will terrify you, because of men’s blood and for the violence done to the land, to every city and to those who dwell in them.
verses.arminianNotes: “For the violence done to Lebanon will overwhelm you.” Arminian readers note that Babylon’s violence reached forests and animals as well as people, and they see God holding the conqueror responsible for harm done to creation and cities alike.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s concern for land, animals, and cities as part of his rule over all creation, and read the overwhelming judgment as fitting recompense. Shared ground: both traditions note that Lebanon was prized for its cedars, which conquerors often felled, though no specific event is named, and both see the refrain from 2:8 as sealing the verdict.

verses.text: “What value does the engraved image have, that its maker has engraved it; the molten image, even the teacher of lies, that he who fashions its form trusts in it, to make mute idols?
verses.arminianNotes: “What value does the engraved image have, that its maker has engraved it?” The fifth woe mocks idols. Arminian readers stress the folly of trusting what one’s own hands have made, “the teacher of lies,” which cannot speak or guide.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the idol as the natural end of a heart that worships its own strength (1:11, 16): the maker trusts the thing he made. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as satire on idolatry, compare similar prophetic mockery in Isaiah 44:9–20, and see “mute idols” as the opposite of the LORD who answers his prophet.

verses.text: Woe to him who says to the wood, ‘Awake!’ or to the mute stone, ‘Arise!’ Shall this teach? Behold, it is overlaid with gold and silver, and there is no breath at all within it.
verses.arminianNotes: “Woe to him who says to the wood, ‘Awake!’ or to the mute stone, ‘Arise!’” Arminian readers see the tragic irony of crying out to objects that cannot hear, however richly they are overlaid with gold and silver.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress the final phrase, “there is no breath at all within it,” as the decisive contrast with the living God who gives breath to all. Shared ground: both traditions read the woe as exposing the emptiness of idolatry, and both see the costly overlay of precious metals as outward splendor covering inner lifelessness.

verses.text: But the LORD is in his holy temple. Let all the earth be silent before him!”
verses.arminianNotes: “But the LORD is in his holy temple. Let all the earth be silent before him!” Arminian readers hear the climax of the woes: in contrast to mute idols, the living LORD reigns, and the fitting human response is reverent silence and trust.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD enthroned in his temple, often taken as his heavenly dwelling, as the sovereign before whom every empire falls silent. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the answer to the idols of verses 18–19, compare Zephaniah 1:7 and Zechariah 2:13, and hear a call to awe that prepares for the prayer of chapter 3.
